The Forbidden City. A massive imperial palace complex in central Beijing, China, built during the Ming Dynasty from 1406 to 1420 as the residence of Chinese emperors and the administrative heart of imperial governance.

Named "forbidden" because commoners were forbidden entry without imperial permission, it sprawls across one hundred seventy-eight acres and contains nearly one thousand buildings. They are organized into nested courtyards and gardens, representing the apex of classical Chinese architecture and the cosmological order.

Constructed under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty, it replaced the Yuan Dynasty's capital elsewhere and established Beijing as the capital city.

The complex contains approximately nine hundred eighty buildings across one hundred eight acres of walled grounds, organized by function—administrative, residential, and ceremonial—within hierarchically nested courtyards.

The spatial layout embodies Chinese cosmological principles. The main north-south axis aligns with the north celestial pole, and the emperor's residence is positioned at the cosmic center.

It served as home and workplace for twenty-four emperors across the Ming, from 1368 to 1644, and the Qing dynasties, from 1644 to 1912. This encompasses nearly five hundred years of imperial history.

The complex remained physically isolated from Beijing's urban grid due to protective walls, creating a "forbidden" zone separate from ordinary city life. Its geography within Beijing—positioned at the city's center along the north-south axis—reflected imperial ideology, making it both a physical structure and a spatial embodiment of centralized Chinese authority.

The Forbidden City suffered damage during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900, foreign occupation, and the Chinese Civil War. It now stands as a UNESCO World Heritage site and major museum, opened to the public in 1949.
